The first file I created was called README — which felt a little too confident for someone who, an hour earlier, still had to look up the difference between let and const.
I sat down with a half-cold cup of coffee, a browser full of beginner tutorials, and a terminal window that seemed to expect me to already know what I was doing. At the top of the screen, my new repository blinked its name back at me: Welcome to My JavaScript Journey.
I’m not new to programming — Python and C++ have kept me company for a while now — but JavaScript was uncharted territory, and starting over always asks for a little courage. I wasn’t feeling especially brave yet, but I liked the idea of leaving a trail.
This wasn’t going to be a place for perfect code. That was the promise I made before typing anything else. It would hold my notes, my messy practice exercises, small projects that would probably break twice before working once, and experiments that started with nothing more than “what happens if I try this?”
I wrote down what I actually wanted to learn — fundamentals first, since skipping them once had already betrayed me, then intermediate ideas, the DOM, browser development, and eventually OOP. The list looked simple. The road behind each word did not.
My finger hovered over the keyboard longer than it needed to. The first commit should have been easy — a few lines, a beginning — but it felt like saying, out loud, that I was serious this time. So I typed the welcome message, read it back once, and moved on.
The First Thing I Learned
Staring at that README, I realized something: writing about learning JavaScript is not the same as learning it. The welcome message was safe. It was plain text. It couldn’t break, and it couldn’t throw an error at me in bright red letters.
So I opened my first real lesson.
Clean layout, short explanations, friendly examples — the kind that make programming look easier than it feels from the other side of the screen. The topic was variables. More specifically, let and const.
At first, I thought I had it figured out. let was for values that could change. const was for values that should stay the same. Simple enough — almost too simple. Then I started overthinking it. What did "should stay the same" actually mean? Was const a rule, or just a suggestion? Would JavaScript really stop me if I broke it? I hadn't written a single line of real code yet, and I was already negotiating with two keywords like they were a life decision.
Still, I wanted to type something myself — not copy, not paste, actually type — so I created a new file and gave it a name that was probably more basic than it needed to be: variables.js.
let name = "Beginner";
const language = "JavaScript";console.log(name);
console.log(language);Four lines. Almost nothing. But I sat there for a second like I’d just laid the foundation of a house. There was a name, a language, and two commands asking the computer to show me both.
Of course, it didn’t work the first time.
I don’t remember the exact mistake — wrong folder, maybe, or a command typed half a second too fast — but I remember the feeling: that small drop in your stomach when something breaks and you don’t have enough experience yet to know if it’s a tiny problem or a huge one. I checked the file name. I checked the folder. I read the lesson again, then typed the command more carefully.
This time, the terminal answered:
Beginner
JavaScriptTwo words. But they felt different, because they hadn’t come from a tutorial — they’d come from my file, in my repository, from code I’d written myself. For the first time, the terminal felt less like a locked door and more like something I could learn to speak to.
Next, I tried changing name:
name = "Still learning";
console.log(name);That worked. So, naturally, I tried the same thing with language:
language = "Python";JavaScript said no.
That error taught me more than the lesson had. const wasn't decoration — it was a promise that the value wouldn't be reassigned, and when I tried to break it, the program held the line. I deleted the offending code and left myself a note instead:
// let can change
// const cannot be reassignedNot a textbook explanation. Just something that made sense to me, in that moment, in that file.
Then I went back to the terminal for my first real commit — not the README, not the announcement that I planned to learn, but actual code, even if it was only a few lines.
Add first JavaScript variables practicePressing enter felt different this time. That commit wasn’t proof that I understood JavaScript — not yet. It was proof that I’d moved from planning to practicing: opened a lesson, written code, made a mistake, fixed it, and kept the evidence.
For a first day, that was enough. Honestly, it was more than enough to keep going.

Following along? I’m documenting everything in my private JavaScript Journey repository for now — broken attempts and all. I plan to make it public once it’s ready. If you’re learning too, I’d love to hear what tripped you up on your first day.
